0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how this is translated in Psalm 4:1. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]
See how you translated the term **testimony** in the superscription to Psalm 8.

1.note: Asaph is speaking as if God were a **Shepherd of Israel**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Caretaker of Israel]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. See how you as a team have decided to translate imperatives in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. For more information on how to translate imperatives see the Psalm 80 Introduction. Alternate translation: [please pay attention]
Asaph is using the phrase **give ear** to mean “listen to me.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

The point of this comparison is that just as a shepherd leads and cares for a flock, so God leads and cares for the descendants of Joseph. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the one caring for the descendants of Joseph as a shepherd cares for a flock]

Here, **Joseph** represents all the people of Israel, particularly the northern tribes descended from Joseph. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Joseph]

Asaph is speaking as if God were one who sits on the cherubim. This refers to God being enthroned above the ark of the covenant. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You who are enthroned above the cherubim]

2.note: Here, **To the face of** represents being in front of or in the presence of these tribes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [In the presence of Ephraim]

Here Asaph is speaking of God displaying his **might** as if it were something that was sleeping and needed to be told to **awaken.** Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [display] or [take action by using]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **might**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and display your power]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to save us]

3.note: This phrase indicates that what follows, **let us be saved**, is the purpose or goal of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [and make your face shine so that we will be saved]

Asaph is speaking as if God’s face were a light that could shine. This represents God showing favor and blessing to his people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and show us your favor]

The expression **let us be saved** is a passive verbal form. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and rescue us]

4.note: Here Asaph is using the possessive form **God of armies** to mean “God, the one who commands the armies of heaven.” It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God who commands armies]

Asaph is using the question form to express strong emotion. If you would not use a rhetorical question for this purpose in your language, you could translate his words as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have smoldered against the prayer of your people for far too long!]

Asaph is speaking as if God’s anger were fire that continues to **smolder**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will you remain angry at]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prayer**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when your people pray to you]

5.q: הֶ֭אֱכַלְתָּ⁠ם לֶ֣חֶם דִּמְעָ֑ה וַ֝⁠תַּשְׁקֵ֗⁠מוֹ בִּ⁠דְמָע֥וֹת שָׁלִֽישׁ
5.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [You have made them eat and drink tears abundantly]
The pronoun **them** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You have made the people of Israel eat]

Asaph is speaking as if tears were **bread** that people could eat. This means that sorrow has become their constant experience. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [food of sorrow]

Asaph is speaking as if **tears** were a liquid that people could drink in great quantity. This means that God has caused the people to experience overwhelming sorrow. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you have caused them to weep an overwhelming amount]

Asaph uses the phrase **in triple measure** as an exaggeration for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use another way to express this emphasis. Alternate translation: [much more than we deserve]

6.note: The first-person pronoun **us** here indicates a shift from the third person **them** in the previous verse. Asaph is now including himself among the suffering people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use the same person as in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [You have made them strife to their neighbors]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strife**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a cause of quarreling with our neighbors]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and our enemies mock us among themselves]

7.note: Here Asaph is using the possessive form **God of armies** to mean “God, the one who commands the armies of heaven.” It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. See how you translated this in verse 4. Alternate translation: [God who commands armies]

The word **and** indicates that what follows, **let us be saved**, is the purpose or goal of what came before. See how you translated this in 80:3. Alternate translation: [and make your face shine so that we will be saved]
Asaph is speaking as if God’s face were a light that could shine. See how you translated this in 80:3. Alternate translation: [and show us your favor]
If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and rescue us]

8.q: גֶּ֭פֶן מִ⁠מִּצְרַ֣יִם תַּסִּ֑יעַ תְּגָרֵ֥שׁ גּ֝וֹיִ֗ם וַ⁠תִּטָּעֶֽ⁠הָ
8.note: The structure here indicates events in sequence. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could show this relationship by using a fuller phrase. Alternate translation: [You pulled up a vine from Egypt, and then you drove out nations and planted it]

Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a **vine**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [You pulled up a nation like a vine from Egypt]

9.note: The structure here indicates events in sequence. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could show this relationship by using a fuller phrase. Alternate translation: [Then you cleared the ground for it, and it took root and filled the land]
The pronoun **it** refers to the vine (representing Israel). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to the face of the vine]

Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a vine that became established and spread. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and the people became established and filled the land]

The phrase **rooted its roots** is an idiom using a verb and noun from the same root. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use an expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it became deeply rooted]

10.note: Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a vine whose shadow covered the mountains. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [The people spread even over the mountains]

The expression **were covered** is a passive verbal form. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Its shadow covered the mountains]

Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a vine whose branches were like the mighty cedars. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and the people became as strong as the mighty cedars]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe the **cedars** as being characterized by extraordinary greatness, as if they belong to God. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [were very great cedars]

11.note: Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a vine that **sent out its branches**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this in another way. Alternate translation: [The people extended their territory]

Asaph is referring to the entire promised land by naming its two extreme boundaries, **the sea** (the Mediterranean Sea in the west) and **the River** (the Euphrates River in the east). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Mediterranean Sea, and its shoots to the Euphrates River]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the sentence if it would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and it sent out its shoots to the River]

12.q: לָ֭⁠מָּה פָּרַ֣צְתָּ גְדֵרֶ֑י⁠הָ וְ֝⁠אָר֗וּ⁠הָ כָּל־עֹ֥בְרֵי דָֽרֶךְ
12.note: In this context, the second phrase states the result of what the first phrase describes. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [You have broken down its walls with the result that all the ones passing on the way pluck it]

Asaph is using the question form to express strong emotion. If you would not use a rhetorical question for this purpose in your language, you could translate his words as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not have broken down its walls]

Asaph is speaking as if Israel were a vineyard with **walls** that God has broken down. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [have you removed its protection]
The pronoun **its** refers to the vine (representing Israel). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the walls of the vine] or [our walls]

The phrase **all the ones passing on the way** is a generalization to emphasize how vulnerable the vine has become. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [so that many people passing by pluck it]

13.q: יְכַרְסְמֶ֣⁠נָּֽה חֲזִ֣יר מִיָּ֑עַר וְ⁠זִ֖יז שָׂדַ֣י יִרְעֶֽ⁠נָּה
13.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Wild animals from the forest and the field ravage and consume it]

13.q: יְכַרְסְמֶ֣⁠נָּֽה חֲזִ֣יר מִיָּ֑עַר וְ⁠זִ֖יז שָׂדַ֣י יִרְעֶֽ⁠נָּה
13.note: Asaph continues to draw an extended comparison between the nation of Israel, and a vineyard planted by a gardener. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the comparison. [Their enemies have destroyed your people like wild animals that root and destroy a vineyard]
The pronoun **it** refers to the vine, which represents Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [ravages the vine … grazes on it]

14.note: Here, **God of armies** describes God as the one who commands the armies of heaven. See how you translated this in 80:4. Alternate translation: [God who commands armies]

Asaph is speaking of Israel as if it were a **vine**. Your language may have a comparable expression you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and care for this people]

15.note: In the phrase **even the stock that your right hand has planted**, Asaph continues to extend the comparison between Israel and a vine. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the comparison. Alternate translation: [even the nation that you have established]

Here, **your right hand** represents God’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you powerfully planted]

Here, **the son** could refer to: (1) the vine, representing the people of Israel. Alternate translation: [the people] or [the nation] or (2) a particular leader of the people of Israel. Alternate translation: [the leader]

16.note: Asaph is speaking of Israel’s destruction as if the vine had been **burned with fire** and **cut down**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It is destroyed, it is cut off]

The expressions **It is burned with fire** and **it is cut down** are passive verbal expressions. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Enemies have burned it with fire and cut it down]

Here, **your face** represents God’s presence and judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [because you rebuke them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rebuke**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are angry with them]

The pronoun shifts from the singular **it** (the vine) to the plural **they** (the people of Israel). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel perish]

17.note: Here, **hand** represents power and protection. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let your protection be on]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the one whom you have chosen and strengthened]

The expressions **on the man of your right hand** and **on the son of man you strengthened for yourself** both describe the same figure. This could refer to: (1) the nation of Israel as a whole, Alternate translation: [on the people at your right hand, on the ones you strengthened for yourself] or (2) to a particular leader or king. Alternate translation: [on the man of your right hand, on the one you strengthened for yourself]

Here, **right hand** represents a position of strength and honor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [on the man you have placed in a position of honor]

Here Asaph is using the phrase **son of man** as a common expression of the culture to indicate a person that has the characteristic of being human. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the human being]

18.note: Here, **And** introduces a vow or promise that Asaph makes as a consequence of God’s intervention. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Then we will not turn back from you]

Asaph is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with the phrase **turn back from you**. He means that if God acts on their behalf, they will continue to live the way God wants his people to live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [And we will continue to live the way you want your people to live]
Here, **your name** represents God himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and we will worship you]

19.note: Here, **God of armies** describes God as the one who commands the armies of heaven. See how you translated this in 80:4. Alternate translation: [God who commands armies]

Here, **and** marks **let us be saved** as the goal or purpose of **Make your face shine**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. See how you translated this in 80:3. Alternate translation: [Make your face shine so that we will be saved]
Asaph is speaking as if God’s face were a light that could shine. See how you translated this in 80:3. Alternate translation: [Show us your favor]

The phrase **let us be saved** is a passive verbal form. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and rescue us]
